Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Lebanon and he appeals a negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated July 14, 2015.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Lebanon and he appeals a negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated July 14, 2015.

Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or the Act), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the RPD's determination that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. Background

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that the Hezbollah group wanted to recruit him when he was approximately 22 years old, and they told him that he must report for training at the end of XXXX 2001. Fearing recruitment by Hezbollah, he left Lebanon and arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2001 on a work permit to work at his uncle's XXXX in Canada. He managed to secure several renewals of his work permit on an annual or bi-annual basis.
The Appellant unsuccessfully tried to get landed status in Canada which was denied due to insufficient points.
The Appellant claimed refugee protection on May 5, 2015, and in early XXXX 2015 he learned from his mother that his youngest brother, XXXX XXXX, was kidnapped by Hezbollah.
He does not want to return to Lebanon because he fears recruitment by Hezbollah and, if recruited, Hezbollah will compel him to fight in Lebanon, Syria and possibly Libya.
Despite his age (36 years), he believes that the Hezbollah would force him to join them because he is physically fit, he is a martial arts expert, and he speaks English.

The Appellant requests that the RAD allow the appeal and find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a protected person. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a different panel. Issues

The Appellant's issues1 are: "Did the RPD panel member apply the proper test as it relates to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)?" and "Did the RPD panel member base his decision on erroneous findings of fact?" Role of the RAD/Standard of Review

The Appellant submitted in his Memorandum that "...no deference is owed by the RAD to RPD decisions since the RAD has to make an independent assessment of the evidence and can substitute its own determination that in its opinion should have been made."

The jurisprudence on the appropriate standard of review or the role of the RAD is still evolving but, at present, the following decision of Justice Phelan is widely accepted and followed. Justice Phelan, in Huruglica,2 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. That decision states: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

Guided by this decision, I will consider the evidence to determine whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. I will also recognize and respect the credibility findings of the RPD where it enjoyed a particular advantage. New Evidence on Appeal
The Appellant provided two affidavits, one from himself and another from his brother. Both of these documents were prepared in XXXX 2015.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to have presented at the time of the rejection.
The burden is on the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of ss.110(4), and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.

The Federal Court has clarified that ss. 110(4) establishes a disjunctive test. The RAD has to consider whether the proposed new evidence arose after the rejection of the refugee claims; if so, the evidence meets the requirements of the section, and is accepted as new evidence. If it did not arise after the rejection, the RAD must consider whether the evidence was reasonably available for presentation to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims; if it was not reasonably available at that time, it meets the requirements of ss.110(4).

If the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim by the RPD, and it was reasonably available, the RAD must consider whether the Appellants could reasonably have been expected, in their circumstances, to have presented the evidence to the RPD prior to the rejection of their claims. If they could not have been expected to do so, the evidence meets the requirements of the section.

If the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claims, was reasonably available, and could reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to be presented to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims, the evidence does not meet the test in section 110(4). The RAD does not have discretion to admit such evidence.

Therefore, ss. 110(4) provides Appellants with an opportunity to provide evidence that they were unable to present to the RPD because the evidence either did not exist prior to the rejection of the claim by the RPD, or because it did exist but was unavailable, or because it did exist and was available, but the Appellants could not have been expected to present it to the RPD.

None of the information contained in the two affidavits provided by the Appellant arose after the rejection of the claim. In fact, these documents repeat the information that was already before the RPD. Moreover, the Appellant did not provide reasonable explanation as to why this information was not available prior to the rejection, or any reasons why the Appellant could not have been expected to present it to the RPD.
Since there is no new evidence accepted by the RAD, the RAD will consider the merits of the appeal based on the Record and the Appellant's Memorandum.
As directed by the Court in Huruglica, I will recognize and respect the RPD's credibility findings, and consider the totality of evidence before me.

The Appellant's alleged fear is from Hezbollah forcing him to join their organization. The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim, finding that the Appellant is not credible. The RPD placed some weight on the Appellant's testimony that he did not call his mother to inquire whether his brother has been released by Hezbollah or not. The Appellant submits that he provided reasonable explanation, that being, that he was afraid to speak to his mother on the phone3. The Appellant submits that the RPD ignored the evidence. I am not persuaded. The RPD considered the Appellant's evidence at length and provided exact wording in paragraph 9 of RPD's Reasons which goes as follows: The Panel: Why did you not call, use the internet or write a letter to find out if XXXX had been released? Have you asked that? The Claimant: No; because I was afraid. I was afraid to speak on the phone to talk about my brother. Take him or he come back [sic]. Busy with my refugee claim. The Panel: You too busy with your refugee claim to find out if your youngest brother had been released by his captors? Is that what you're telling me? The Claimant: Yes sir. And then shortly thereafter: The Claimant: I was thinking about my refugee claim. It was my mistake not to call them. I did not know what to ask. The Panel: Why did you not call and ask whether your brother was still in captivity? This would be easy to answer yes or no so why not call and ask? The Claimant: Because I wasn't thinking about it...

The Appellant clearly testified that he was not thinking about calling his brother, and that he was too busy with his refugee claim. It is true that he did say that he was afraid to speak on the phone; however, that statement is based on the speculation that Hezbollah may be monitoring the telephone. There is no credible evidence to corroborate the Appellant's concern that Hezbollah may be monitoring the telephone line.

The RPD also noted in its Reasons at paragraph 10 that, "The alleged abduction of the younger brother is an important aspect of the claim. It arguably shows that Hezbollah is still actively recruiting people in the claimant's own backyard (so to speak) despite the fact that 14 years have elapsed since he was a prospective recruit."

I note that the documentary evidence clearly states that Hezbollah does not force people to join them. Objective documentary evidence4 shows that: ...Hezbollah's 'Jihad Assembly' is in charge of recruitment...[and that]... full party membership to Hezbollah is offered to recruits based on their allegiance to Hezbollah's ideology... [and that] although Hezbollah exerts 'general political and social influence to encourage people to join,' Hezbollah does not 'forcibly recruit members'. [Emphasis added] ...' although [Hezbollah is] very powerful, they generally don't threaten or interfere with people on an individual basis; unless that person is a security threat to them, or has done something to one of their members.'... if Hezbollah is 'after' someone, there is 'no protection in Lebanon'. [Emphasis added]

Thus, the evidence shows that Hezbollah does not force people to join and does not bother individuals for recruitment purposes. I recognize that there is no protection in Lebanon for anyone who is a target of Hezbollah; however, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that Hezbollah is not interested in the Appellant. Even if I were to accept the Appellant's allegation that the RPD did not consider all of the evidence, I have reviewed all of the evidence and find that the outcome for the Appellant does not change. Documentary evidence clearly contradicts the Appellant's allegation that the Hezbollah is keen to force him to join them.

I have also considered other similar groups and find that Lebanon has numerous groups and the documentary evidence does not show that any of these groups force individuals to join them. For example, documents5 show: START reports that, '[w]hile Hamas, Hezbollah, and al-Fatah generally dominate, smaller, more extreme groups, such as Asbat al-Ansar, operate on the fringes and draw membership from individuals alienated by the larger outfits' (n.d.a). Asbat al-Ansar is also known as 'Osbat Al Ansar, Usbat Al Ansar, Esbat Al- Ansar, Isbat Al Ansar, Usbat-ul-Ansar, Band of Helpers, Band of Partisans, League of the Followers'....In 2002, Asbat al-Ansar was designated a terrorist entity in Canada (ibid.). The United States also designated the group as a "foreign terrorist organization" in 2002. ...Asbat al-Ansar is a Sunni 'extremist' group that was formed in the 'late 1980s or early 1990s by Sheik Hisham Shreidi, a Palestinian refugee and preacher'.

Another such group is generally known as AMAL and documentary evidence6 states: ...Amal is an acronym for 'Afwaj al-Muqawa al-Lubnaniyah' (START n.d.; Political Handbook of the World 2013), which, according to the PoliticalHandbook of the World, means 'Groups of the Lebanese Resistance' (ibid.). The word Amal also means "hope" in Arabic. The International Crisis Group adds that 'Amal has followed in Hizbollah's footsteps at every stage of escalating domestic tensions'. According to the Professor, the Amal Movement does not 'forcibly recruit' people (Professor 6 Dec. 2013). The Professor indicated that Amal often recruits youth from Shi'a backgrounds 'who are mostly secular' and 'are attracted to Amal.'[Emphasis added]

The RPD found that the Appellant's explanation for his delay in claiming protection of 14 years, that he wanted to return to Lebanon, was not reasonable. The Appellant argues that the "Appellant's explanation was reasonable. He was [also] afraid to tell people he had been approached by Hezbollah, a terrorist group." I am not persuaded. His actions are not consistent with his testimony that he wanted to return to Lebanon. If the Appellant wanted to go back to Lebanon, why was he trying vigorously to remain in Canada by several different processes? This does not make sense. If the Appellant was afraid to return due to Hezbollah, it would be reasonable to expect that he would have sought protection in Canada a long time ago, especially considering the fact that if "Hezbollah is 'after' someone, there is 'no protection in Lebanon'."

Regarding the Appellant's other issue, "did the RPD panel member apply the proper test as it relates to sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA", the Appellant does not clearly spell out where and how the RPD erred. The burden is on the Appellant to provide:7 ...full and detailed submissions regarding (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the Refugee Protection Division
The Appellant did not fulfill his burden as he did not state where and how the RPD erred by applying the wrong test. Therefore, I find that this issue has no merit.
Therefore, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, as it is supportable pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Act.
Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

This appeal is therefore dismissed. (signed) "Atam Uppal" Atam Uppal September 28, 2015 Date 1 Exhibit P-2, Appellant's Record, Memorandum, p. 19. 2 Huruglica, Bujar v. M.C.I. (F.C., no. IMM-6362-13), Phelan, August 22, 2014; 2014 FC 799. 3 Exhibit P-2, Appellant's Record, Memorandum, p. 25, para. 15. 4 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD's Record, National Documentation Package (NDP) for Lebanon (28 November 2014), item 4.2, Lebanon: Hezbollah, including areas of operation, political involvement, military activity, recruitment practices, treatment of citizens and state protection. 5 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD's Record, NDP for Lebanon (28 November 2014), item 4.7, LBN104844.E. 6 Ibid., item 4.8, LBN104694.E. 7 Refugee Appeal Division Rules, 3(3)(g)(i)(ii). --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ RAD.25.02 (June 23, 2014) RAD File No. / N° de dossier de la SAR : TB5-08137
